blocks.x: Okay, it's going. Well, we ready? Yep.

Well, this is Edgar Mosley, Edgar P. Mosley. When were you born? I was born in Yarlene, Louisiana. You remember the exact date now? I was born in 1895, 12 days of November, and at least make me 62 years old now.
What part of the town were you born in?
Born in on the Algiers side. Over there?
In Algiers. Yes, I knew you lived there.
Well, the Algiers is just same as Yarlene. Yes, it's part of the city. And I started playing music. I started out in 1925.
When you were a boy, did you play any instrument at all when you were a kid?
No, I didn't. No harmonica. That's what I mean. That's an instrument there.
Or even a little tin pipe.

Well, I used to play a harmonica when I was a kid. I played that for long until I got to be a man, young man. Then I started out taking lessons with drums in 1925. And in 26, I started out, I mean, in 26, I started out with Howard.
Mm-hmm. Oh, you might tell a bit about your family, too. Did any of your parents or brothers or older brothers or anyone play?
Yeah, I have a brother who's a drummer just like me. Is he older than you?
I know many of you.
Older than me. John Mosley. Mm-hmm. I'm his, I'm 50, I'm 62 and he is 64. That's a couple of years. He's two years older than me.
Had your father played any?
My father used to play harmonica and guitar. Yeah? Get-tar, too? Yeah, harmonica and guitar.
Did he work with any of the bands with his guitar?
No, he didn't. No more than him and a friend he had me called Newt. Newt was to play the guitar most of the time. He'd blow the harmonica. Well, that's the kind of music he played. Yeah.
Had your mother played anything? Who, my mother?
No, she didn't. Did she sing much?
I guess everybody sang a little bit. Nothing but sing church hymns.
Which church did you belong to? She belongs to the Catholic Church in Algiers. We're always Catholic. Yes.
Can you remember some of the early music you heard when you were a boy, the very first, I guess, of course, your father playing the harmonica and guitar? Well. Any bands or parades?

During that time, my father was playing. I didn't remember those numbers then because my father had been dead a long time. He died when I was ten years old. That'd make me remember none of the tunes. You wouldn't remember very much. No, but I know one tune he used to play all the time. I was small, but after the ball was over. Oh, yeah. Yeah, he played that. And another one, he used to play the old Chicken Reel. Chicken Reel.
Oh, yeah.
Chicken Reel.
I got the orchestration from that. Yeah. The old Robichaux band, Maurice Duran had some of Robichaux's music and he sold me a bunch of it all years ago.

Yeah, well, I remember them two old numbers good when he used to play. I was a small kid, but I remember them good. Them the two numbers even that form. No, I don't remember the others. But for the other band, I tell you, there's a lot of numbers they played. You're trying to get your work finished up. And I can't recall the NAMM back from way back. There's a lot of numbers I played with Bunk Johnson. And they were so old back. He know them all. Oh, yeah, he knew them. And right now, if he's sitting down playing, they'll come right to me. But for the NAMM of them, I couldn't call them.
You said Blue Bell's Goodbye was one I believe.
That was one of them, yeah.
I got the sheet music with that up here in the store.
Yeah. Blue Bell's Goodbye. Yeah, that was one of his numbers. I never heard of him. But Bunk's had more old numbers, I think, than any old numbers. I mean, that he kept track of.
Yeah, he could remember all of them.

He could, yeah. I never forgot of him. Yeah. I played, oh, a lot of dances with him. When we made your record, huh? We had a job to play. He played a job with us at night, yeah. And he was quite a nice fellow to be with.
Yeah, he was a good trumpet player. He remembered all of his old times. Yeah.
And...
How come you wanted to take up drums? I mean, it's a natural instrument to take up, but most of the real young boys, you know, they all want to play drums.
Yeah, well, I'll tell you. I first started with clarinet. Oh, really?
I tried to learn clarinet.

Yeah. But I'd get tired holding it up in there. So, yeah. So I'd decide that I'd learn to take up drums. Learn drums. Well, at the time of learning the drums, Kit Howard used to come by and Howard, well, he tried to show me a lot of it.
Well, he'd been playing drums, hadn't he?

He had been playing drums, yeah. Yeah, and he tried to like me. And by me and him being good friends, he took me on a little job where he could get by with me. And then after he got me down, I'd come and say, be good on the drums, good as the bank fella. I played all the job he played. Plum up, tell the last of 43 when I left and came up here.
That's what I wanted to check on. You came out here late in 1943.
That's right, late. I had made them records for you.
Yeah, well, then the next year I came down there. I didn't think you were there. I didn't remember now for sure.
No, I wasn't there. I was in California then. Oh, right.
I didn't know that's when, that's for sure.

Yeah. And after I left from there, left the band, all I certainly missed him when I got up here. It was all the way different when I got up here, you see. But I didn't worry about playing no more. I just started playing back since, I think I started back in 54.
That's the last four years in about.

Yeah, 54 I started back to playing up here. I had to do. Well, they had been at me to play and Howard, he had come up and told Paul's going to try to get me to play. Yeah. Paul's back there now. So, Paul's back in Yorley. No. So, Paul come to me with some fellas and they talked to me and I got together. And from that time on I've been playing ever since.
Did you save your drum set though when you moved out? Did you bring it?

No, the drums I had home, I didn't bring them out here. When I got with them, I bought this set of drums you see I have out there now. Because the drums I had home, I wouldn't bring them, they was too old fashioned.
Yeah.
Everybody had gotten the later style now. So, I figured my brother, he had the drums back home. Well, your brother still has them.
He still plays. There was one, I saw him in a parade this year, about April. Yeah. It was in April with Howard. Yeah. And he had the old, I believe it was called Silverleaf. Uh huh.
Silverleaf brass band. Yeah. On his bass drum. Was that yours? No, that was hitting a little black bass drum. That's his bass drum. Mine was a bigger drum.
But he used in the orchestra and all that.
Yeah, mine was a bigger drum. Well, I left the whole thing with him. I went back down there in 49 and said about he'd come back in 51. I played with him when I was down there then.
Oh, did you stay for a couple of years?

I stayed for one year and five months. Oh, I didn't know you were there. Yeah, and I came back up here. Uh huh. And after I came back up with my mother down in 52, and I went back to see her and I haven't been back since.
When you started on drums, did you live across the river then?
No, I lived in the city. Where was it you?
That's what I mean, over in New Orleans.

I lived in New Orleans. But I lived on the other side of the river where I was born at down on the other side of the river in Algiers in McLendonville. That's right below Algiers. Down the coast they call it. Down there where George Lewis lived. Yeah.
Well, it wasn't as far as the Cut-Off, what they call the Cut-Off.
No, I wasn't born at the Cut-Off. I was born right along, a little past where George Lewis lived. Where George Lewis lived.

You ought to see that place now. It's all grown up. Yeah. Hundreds of houses in there. Yeah. They have the new bridge now. Uh-huh. So they're developing all of that. They built up hundreds of houses, all those streets past. George was the last house there when he built it.
Uh-huh.
And now there's a hundred of them past him.

Yeah. Well, the place I was born, we was living right on the river. House built right on that side of the river, right by the, under, when the water's reds, was, uh, be all under the building. Oh, yeah. Well, I was born right there on the river side. And that'd been a long time ago. Yeah. Yeah.
When did you move over to New Orleans then?
Well, I moved over in Yarlene. When I moved to New Orleans, I moved to New Orleans in about 1923. Right before you started on the river.
Yeah. When I moved to New Orleans.
And I got over there and I made friends with Howard and all of them when I liked the city and I stayed over there.
Was that St. Philip or DuMaine Street you were living on the time that year?
That was St. Philip between Ramport and St. Claude.
I knew it was up in there somewhere.
Yeah. And Howard. What was the house number?
Remember that now?
What, what that house number was? 1131. 1131. 1131.
I probably had with my old north.
Yeah.
1121. 1121. I remember. Been a good while, you know. 1121. Now, Howard was living right across the street from here. Yeah, that's right.
Yeah.
Jim Robinson too, wasn't he? Jim Robinson was staying across that.
Or close there anyway.
No, he wasn't staying across the street then. He was on Marais first. He was on Marais first.
He was on Marais street then. One time he lived in a double house, though, after that. He did.

Yeah. And then after I left, due to war, he was staying with Kid Howard. Yeah, that's what I mean, he moved. Yeah, that's when he stayed across the street from, but I had left then. Yeah, you left then. Uh, so I played with a lot of fellas.
Jim Hill was up in that section there too. Yeah.

The bass player. The bass player was, he was down between Libby and Marais. Yeah, he was there. Yeah, I think he's still there yet if you all can move. No, he moved this summer. Did he? I don't know where. I don't have his address. Oh, yeah. Jim Robinson knows, I'm sure.
I haven't found out where he lives.
Yeah. Just moved this summer.
Uh-huh. Yeah, and I played with a lot of them. I played with Kid Rene. I know you heard of Kid Rene.

Sure, yeah. He made some records, right? And I played with Chris Kelly. Oh, yeah. Parade, though. I played a lot of Parade with Chris Kelly and Rene. Of course, Rene and Chris Kelly had their drums. But I was a two-way band. I would play trap drum, snare drum, eat a bass drum, anything they wanted. The few of them I played. When you played with Kid Rene, for instance, who else was in the band? Can you remember sort of the lineup any time? Oh, no. I know they all changed, but can you remember the band? Oh, no. Can you remember the band? Can you remember the band? Oh, no. Can you remember the band? Yeah.
Can you remember the band? Oh, no. Can you remember the band? Yeah. Can you remember the band? Yeah. Yeah. I know they all changed, but can you remember some of the band?
Well, it was, uh, Mealy Hawkins was on trumpet. What was that?
I don't even know him.
Mealy, you know, he's home now, right? He was, he was fooling around with trumpet when we was there, but he never did get good. He didn't follow it up like Howard now. What's the last name?
Mealy Hawkins.
Hawkins?
Yeah, Mealy Hawkins.

Well, I have to try to find him. And they had, uh, Rene was on trumpet. Mealy Hawkins was on trumpet. They had another fella named Joe, I can't call his last name. He was, I had three trumpets. Can't call this other Joe's name. Was it Joe Phillips or something? No, a little short, bright fella. No, I don't know. Well, we had, we had Sonny Henry on Trimboine. He'll play with the Eureka now. Yeah, and we had Joe Abram on Trimboine.
Yeah, he died, you know, a couple years ago. Yeah.
And, uh, we had old man Fels Delmo on, on, on tuba. Oh, you never knew.
Yeah, on tuba. I know you, I don't know if, no, you didn't be around long enough to know him.
He used to be around with all of us. Is he still living? He's still living. He's still living. They tell me he's living, tell me he's looking all right.
He's an old man named One Us, you know.

Yeah, well, I find him and could have interviewed with him. Yeah, and we had Rodgers. Ernest Rodgers. Ernest Rodgers on snare drum with us. Yeah, and we had Rodgers on snare drum with us. Yeah, and we had Rodgers. Ernest Rodgers on snare drum with us. He died three years ago or two years ago this September.
Yeah, and I didn't know if somebody came up here and told me he had died.
And I hadn't even, I moved to New Orleans about four months before that.
Oh. And I never did get out to see him. Yes. And I got to the waiting and I was so mad that self, you know,

himself, you know, for not going to see him. Uh-huh. And you was in the only then? Yeah, I'd been there for four months before he died and I didn't even get out to see him. Oh, yeah. Uh-huh. Now, I didn't know he was sick. I'd heard somebody say he was sick on 10 to go, but then all of a sudden he's dead before we knew him. Yeah, and he was telling me I had George Lewis. George Lewis was us on the clad at this brass band with Rennie. He played E-flat, I guess. Yeah, that's what he played. Yeah, we had a pretty good brass band. We got a lot of white there with it, too. Who was the other drummer sometime with you? Well, my brother used to drum with me. What brother did you get? Sometime Remus Matthews. Oh, yeah. He used to, when I played a job with Remus, Remus, my brother couldn't make it, Remus was playing his place. Then sometime old man Allen, he'd hires to come down there to play a funeral. Well, old man Allen and Remus were this and that drum player. Well, I played bass drum with him in that band.
Then, to go on with something like that with Chris Kelly, if you can remember when you played with him, who he might have used sometime.

Well, Chris been dead a long time. Yeah. And I played with him. Chris knew they were all different fellas. That's the point. He never did have no, none of them had no straight up band, honey. Yeah. They always changed it, man. Because if you got a job for Saturday, and I got a job, and then you hire me, and I'll get a job, pay more. I'll come give you the part of the bank and go over there to the fellow. Well, that meant them just kept on, had always on the run, you know what I mean? The good man's what they wanted to get. When they thought they had them, they had to go get the man they didn't want. Well, that's the way it went. You didn't keep up with the Sandmans all the time.
I was wondering, who might have played trumpet with Chris though? Would he pick out somebody the same style? He didn't have anybody else that style.
Well, then I know nobody played Chris Kelly style. He played...

Now Howard, he played more something like Chris Kelly than any of them. Get out. Because Chris Kelly had a nice tone, Howard had a nice tone, Howard's blowing. But Howard played more like Chris Kelly than any trumpet player I know of in Yawley. And Chris was a good trumpet player.
Yeah, that's what they said.
Also Howard was a good trumpet player.
Especially on blues.
Randy was a good trumpet player. And you take a lot of them fellas down there, all them good trumpet players, well there's quite a few of them passed out.
Oh yeah.
See, like Poinche, he passed out.
Well, Hunch is back there again now.
In Yaw?
Yeah, I sent him a postcard the other day.
Did you? Yeah. Yeah.
He stopped in my place right now.
Yeah, now Buddy P.T., I played with him.
Oh yeah.
But Buddy passed.
Yeah, what kind of a style did he have?

Oh, he had a nice style. He had a different style from any of them. But he had a nice style. He had a real nice style of playing trumpet. And he was a good musician. But he got on sick and he just kept sick, sick. Feel better. He tried to play a job. He'd go out, they'd have to bring him home sick. So he got the place where he didn't bother with it no more.
Yeah, it's too bad. He must have been a wonderful trumpet player.
He was. And the night before he died, he was talking on the corner of St. Philip and St. Claude.
Well, he just died suddenly like that?
Yeah, and the next day I heard he was dead.
And you'd been talking to him the night before?
Yeah, because I played his funeral, you know.
Yeah, if he wasn't sick in bed then, he'd been long.

Well, he was licking sick, you know, walking around sick, yeah. He'd be standing up talking to you sometime. He'd tell you got to go home and lay down. He'd suffer with that sick, sickness a lot. Well, I played.
That was one of the big funerals, I guess. I think Louis Armstrong was there.
He was, he was there. Because me and Howard and George Louis and them, we had the band, we played at the funeral. We made up a band and played at the funeral.
How many bands did they have, more than one? Or?

I think they had two of us. I done forgot, I think they had two bands. The band was practically made up though. You know, to play at the funeral, because he was an old musician, and he was a regular musician. He'd get around with everybody. And all the boys would just get together and make a brass band, play at the funeral. But he had a nice funeral that day.
I'm wondering about the bands across the river. That is like the parades and the brass bands. Like Henry Allen had a band. Did you ever hear Professor Monetta's uncle had a band?

Well, I heard Allen band. I heard his band a lot of times. And they had another band over there. And they were all them fellas. I was about, during that time, and I was about around 11, 12 years old. But I know they had the Atlantic band. They had the Pacific band.
Oh yeah, who had that?

Now, I don't want to say it wrong. I don't know if Allen was the Atlantic or the Pacific, but I believe he was the Atlantic band. I believe Allen had. And there was some more fellas, and I can't call them them. They're all old fellas. All them is D's.
Yeah, we'll go check with some other people down there too.
Yeah, I don't know. I think I know one of them was the Pacific, one was the Atlantic.
Atlantic. I didn't know about the Atlantic.
Yeah, they had the Atlantic band and the Pacific band. And they had them two bands now. They, of course, they're using bands from the Orleans.
Yeah, sure.

Yeah. But they were two brass bands. They used to work all the time from the Orleans to the Algea. They had all the work. They used to do more. They had a lot of art fellas work down there. Parades. Art fellas would parade all the time. That's why Allen learned his son, his son boy, his boy there, how to play trumpet in a parade. He had a parade he played. He had his son right in there with him. Yeah. Yeah.
Did you ever hear that Minetta brass band? I think Professor Minetta's uncle had it.
Yeah, they had a brass band. Do you remember it? Well, that's the brand I'm talking about now. Did he ever tell you the name of the band?
No, I think he called it the Norm. That was his name. Norman, I guess. Norm Minetta brass band. Oh. That might have had another name too.

Well, I small kid, I got their band all right. They had a pretty good band. All them fellas had pretty good good doing them top. See, the people wasn't like this. Nah. The people went for anything. If you just could play a guitar. Oh, yeah. It was all right. But they didn't like that. Nah. Yeah. But they band what they had went over big. Yeah, I know the Minetta band. But I was small.
Yeah, sure.
And also him, he was young himself.
Oh, yeah.
Yeah, he was.
But I think it was his uncle, Professor Minetta's uncle, that really ran the band.
Yeah.

See, Fess is six years older than you. Oh. But his uncle was a good deal older than that. Yeah. I wondered if there was much difference between the music over there. I guess all the same fellas played on each side though.
Oh, Sam. Well, the music then was good. But as it kept coming, coming, coming, the fellas got better and better.
Yeah.
Yeah. Jazz used to be on a style that nobody had all that fancy playing on their trumpet.
Yeah.

They played straight and things. But during the time when Chris Kelly and all of them got together and all, stopped playing, well, that's when the fancy trumpet come in. Yeah. You know, making all the different things. Yeah. But before they used to play straight, they used to play just like Big Landry. Oh, yes. Landry would die. And he never did change his way. He said that same way when what they played way back.
You used to hear him down in Lutzen's with Big Eye.
Yeah. That's the way he played. Never did change his style of playing. But Randy Howard, all them boys, they come on up to the right. They boost up the jazz. And went good too.

I was wondering a little bit about drummers. If you can remember any of the early drummers when you were a boy, before you learned drums even. Can you think of some of the fellows you maybe used to watch?

Oh, I used to watch old man Allen had a brother. He called Sam. Sam Allen, I think his name. He was a drummer. But he was a street drummer. He wasn't no St. Allen drummer. Well, drummers I knowed. I knowed Happy. Oh, yeah.
Was that Red Happy or Happy Goldston?
In Yawling. Yeah. He died.
Yeah, Red Happy.
Yeah. When he was dead. Yeah.
The other one is still living. Played with Celestan's band. After you left.
Well, that Happy died. Yeah. Now this Happy, yeah. He's in Celestan's band now. If he ain't quit.
No, about a year ago he quit. His health hasn't been so good.
Oh, yeah. Well, that Happy, he was playing with Bill Matthews.
Yeah, that's right. Bill Matthews.
Yeah, that's him. Well, this is that Happy I'm talking about.
Yeah, Red Happy.
Yeah, Red Happy.
Bolton, I think was his name. Yeah.
Yeah. And, oh, they had, I know a lot of drummers, but it'd been way back and then really I wasn't playing with them.
No.
At that time, I didn't keep anything. Of course, you know about Lil' Jimmy the drummer. He died too. Yeah. Lil' Jimmy. Yeah. You haven't met him, haven't you?
Yes. What about, did you ever hear old man Contrell, they call him, or Contrell? Contrell, played with P. Rowling and all.
Did you hear him? Contrell, let me see. Yeah, I did hear him a long time ago. He was a pretty nice drummer. Then they had another drummer. I can't call his last name, they called him Clave.
Yeah, I don't know.
Clave, he was a drummer.
Do you remember Henry Zeno?
Yeah, I remember Henry Zeno.
He lived at the Eagle Band.

Yeah. Uptown with Ricky Deucing. Yeah, yeah, I remember him. Oliver too. Yeah, played with Oliver and all. Yeah. Boy, it's a whole lot of drummers. They had a lot of eating down to Royal. Now, Royal, I can't call his last name, but Royal, he was a Sam Morgan drum player.
Oh yeah, I don't remember him.

No, he played with a Sam Morgan band all the time. He traveled with them and all. That was Sam Morgan's drummer, Royal. Oh yeah. Yeah. And he had another drummer he knew before I knew Royal, but this fella did and I don't know his name, see? Because I wasn't playing no drums then. But I went around while they was. I was, but I don't know this fella there. He was a nice drummer.
I was going to ask again about your brother. You say your brother helped you along to show you drums when you started? Or?

No, Howard showed me. Oh Howard, that was Howard. And after I did get on learning, during the time I learned what my brother, he learned but showed me some stuff too. But Howard was playing more regularly than my brother. He showed me quicker than my brother, showed me more than my brother. Because of course my brother's a good drummer too. Yeah.
Yeah.
He played trap drum and parade drum. He played one of them just like me. But I don't think he ever been, he ain't never made no records or nothing.
No, I don't believe so.
No, he didn't. He ain't never made no records or nothing.
He was saying he was going to try to get the old Silverleaf band together again if he could and some of them.
That's my brother? Oh yeah.
That was in April.
Yeah. Well, they need to get something together. I don't think he got the one standard band on there. That's a Ricker band.
Well, it was a young tuxedo.
They got a young tuxedo? Yeah.
With John Kazimer.
Oh, that's right. Because Big Roger was playing here.
Yeah.

The fella was dying. And John Kazimer with the tuxedo and Big Red, he got the E-Rica band. Yeah. Yeah. I used to play with that band too, the E-Rica band. Oh, you did. But I didn't stay with them because I always was traveling with Howard and them, and I didn't have time to be there with them. Because the way they'd get their job, they'd get it when somebody died, or eat a parade, and that wasn't regular enough for me. So I stayed at the orchestra with him. Of course, we played a lot of funerals and things ourselves. And then we'd have a fellas die. They'd pick up the money, and high Howard and play a few. The parade the same way, them clubs, you know. Oh, I don't know.
Who would you say was about the best drummer down there you ever heard? Did you have a favorite?
Well, I tell you, there was some pretty good one down there. No, I couldn't hardly see it this time.
Hard to pick. Hard to pick.

One or two right there. Hard to pick it. Some of them, they all used to get there and fight against one another, you know. Yeah. Yeah, like you'd be playing a job there, two or three drummers come there, and you'd better be good. Because they all come to show you up, see. And you had to play like that, only keep them from showing you up. Well, it was a hard thing to tell. Yeah. Yeah. But they had some pretty good drummers there, which they have some there now. Now, Louie Coleman, boy, he's a nice drummer, but he's not in the jazz business like we all, see. No. He's a young drummer. A little different style. Yeah, that's what I'm talking about. But we was talking about way back, the old drummers, yeah. Yeah, they had some good drummers there. Now, Bill Matthew was a good drummer when he was playing. That's right. Yeah, he was a good drummer.
Never saw him on drums.
Yeah, he started playing when he didn't need pants. I remember when he played the first dance on Belwyn Street.
Over in Algiers?

Yeah, on Belwyn Street. He played the first dance at this Belwyn Park, they call it. And I went back there with a little bit of kid listening at him. He's playing good. And then when I did pick it up to understand he's playing good, but he gave it up and got on the trampoline. Yeah, he was a good drummer too. But they had drummers in the old age better than him. But it's been way back, I can't call any name. Now, Si, he's a good drummer. Si, he's a good drummer. Chester, he's a little late comer, him. Chester's drummer in the old age.
Wait a minute, Chester.
Chester Jones.
Chester Jones.
Oh, Chester Jones.
I was trying to think of Chester Zardes of the bass player. I haven't seen him.
You don't know where he is.
He hasn't been out here.
They say he's in Yorlin. I don't know.
He's supposed to be, but nobody's seen him for several months. About a year now.
Yeah, well, I haven't seen him. Last time I see Chester, that was in 1950.
Oh, where was he then? In the...
He was in Yorlin.
He was in Yorlin.
He was in Yorlin. He was in Yorlin. Because I met him.
This is Philadelphia.
I met him on Liberty and St. Anne. Right on the corner. I mean, it was talk.
Yeah.
And I haven't seen him since. So, I don't know. Maybe he'd have left town. I don't know.
He might have.
Might have.
Might be out in the country or something like that.
Tell him the thing had gotten a little slow down there with music. He might have moved up some.
Might have gone.
Yeah.
He's a good bass player.
Yeah, he is a good bass player. Yeah, he really is a good bass player. And I tell you, slow drag pretty good bass player from back in his age. Right.
From back in his age.
Slow drag picks that thing real fast there with Yorlin there. Yeah.
Got more life than almost anybody.

I'm telling you. But they got a lot of young ones now. Get tired. Can't hold up like he do. Can't do like he do. He really works. He works. Now, that's a man started out. I remember slow drag. I remember slow drag in 1923. I met him. A young fella. He came in and another fella he called George. Sandpaper George. Yeah. Hudson had a horn made out of pipe.
Oh yeah, like a bazooka.

Yeah, they used to go out like, or even night most of them. Get out there and start around and see what could they pick up. They're doing good. Then when I was seeing slow drag in 1923. I made him a bass out of box.
Yeah, I saw that. Yeah.
Yeah, he played out of box. And then I did come to fire way back here lately. He goes stuff
and he got to playing and then Joey Lewis took it. He played good. But he been fooling around with guitar and a thing a long time.
He still can play guitar.
Yeah. He's a nice fella too.
Oh yeah, I like him.
He's a nice fella. Yeah, he is a nice fella.
Well, I must write him a postcard too. A lot of fellas there I was sending some postcards to this morning. I haven't sent one to Drag.
Yeah.

Well, this covers your life I think pretty well. There's another minute or so on there if there's anything else that you can think of about your life. I was going to ask one thing. Did you ever play on any wagons advertising? I saw you on one truck later, you know, in 1943.
Yeah, I played on wagons.
But when you were younger, when you started in 1925, did they have wagons advertising?

They had wagons then. So they had trucks and they had, some people had their furniture wagons. And they put the furniture, I played in the furniture wagons, you know, with our appetite. But it didn't last long after I started out. Probably about to want the truck cause he could get around faster than the truck. And that's why they come in to cutting the wagons out. Cause this old bass player, he hauled us around in this wagon. I can't call his name. He's dead now. He's an old fella. He used to play bass with us. He died. Well, he had a waggon and horse. Well, the musician to try to get him the job, to haul him around so he could make the money. Well, I played in his wagon once. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. I didn't stay in the wagon long. They started getting trucks. After people was able to get trucks, they'd get the trucks. Cause they said they could get around appetite more further and quicker.
Yeah. They were more solid too. Yeah.
Cause see the wagon, you couldn't get around like you want. It was too slow.
Yeah.
But it was alright, appetite in them wagons. But the wagon was good as a truck. Cause some of them wagons was too narrow, you see.
Yeah.
Uh-huh. So they started getting trucks after that. It was a pleasure getting a truck.
Yeah, I suppose.

The best truck to ride in though, the appetite is a truck with the top on. Oh, yeah. See them wagons and them trucking down on top on. The music sounded good to the people, but it was hard to us. Yeah, it was really hard.
Uh-huh.

segments.title: Opening and birth in Algiers, 1895
segments.summary: Mosley states his name and that he was born in Algiers, New Orleans, in November 1895.

segments.title: Harmonica as a boy, then drum lessons in 1925
segments.summary: He played harmonica as a boy, took drum lessons in 1925 and began playing with Kid Howard in 1926.

segments.title: Family: brother John, father's harmonica and guitar, Catholic church
segments.summary: His older brother John is a drummer; his father played harmonica and guitar with a friend Newt; his mother only sang hymns.

segments.title: Father's tunes and old numbers played with Bunk Johnson
segments.summary: He recalls the tunes his father played, then old numbers and dances played with Bunk Johnson.

segments.title: Switching from clarinet to drums with Kid Howard's help
segments.summary: He tried clarinet, tired of holding it up, and learned drums with Kid Howard, who took him on jobs.

segments.title: Leaving for California in 1943, returning to play in 1954
segments.summary: He left the band in 1943, was in California, resumed playing in 1954, and discusses his old drums and brother's Silverleaf band drum.

segments.title: Growing up in McDonoghville near George Lewis
segments.summary: He lived on the river side below Algiers near where George Lewis later lived.

segments.title: Moving to New Orleans in 1923 and musician neighbours on St. Philip
segments.summary: He moved to St. Philip Street around 1923 and recalls where Kid Howard, Jim Robinson and Jim Hill lived.

segments.title: Playing with Kid Rene and Chris Kelly; Rene's band lineup
segments.summary: He played trap, snare and bass drum parades with Chris Kelly and Kid Rene, and lists Rene's trumpets, trombones, tuba and Ernest Rodgers.

segments.title: Chris Kelly's shifting personnel and trumpet style
segments.summary: Kelly's bands changed constantly; Kid Howard played most like Chris Kelly.

segments.title: Buddy Petit's style, illness and funeral
segments.summary: He recalls Buddy Petit's playing, his sickness and sudden death, and the funeral band assembled for it.

segments.title: Algiers brass bands: Henry Allen, Atlantic and Pacific, Minetta
segments.summary: He recalls Algiers brass bands heard as a boy of eleven or twelve.

segments.title: Plain early jazz trumpet versus the fancy style
segments.summary: Early jazz trumpet was played straight, like Big Landry, until Chris Kelly's generation brought the fancy style.

segments.title: Early New Orleans drummers he watched or knew
segments.summary: He names early drummers including Sam Allen, Red Happy, Contrell, Clave, Zeno and Royal of Sam Morgan's band.

segments.title: His brother and Kid Howard as teachers; Silverleaf, Tuxedo and Eureka bands
segments.summary: Howard taught him more than his brother; brother's Silverleaf band, and why he skipped the Eureka band.

segments.title: Favorite drummers, drummers' competition, Bill Matthews
segments.summary: Drummers competed to show each other up; he comments on Louie Coleman, Bill Matthews and Chester Jones.

segments.title: Whereabouts of bassist Chester Zardis, and Slow Drag
segments.summary: They discuss where Chester Zardis went and praise his bass playing, and Slow Drag's.

segments.title: Slow Drag Pavageau in 1923, Sandpaper George and homemade instruments
segments.summary: He remembers meeting Slow Drag in 1923, Sandpaper George, and a bass he made out of a box.

segments.title: Playing advertising wagons and trucks
segments.summary: He describes playing on furniture wagons and then trucks to advertise dances, and how the trucks replaced wagons.
